channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: China wants you to cheer for the robots taking your job | E2329
gist: Jason Calacanis and co-host Lon read Beijing's World Humanoid Robot Games (two human world records broken across 51 events) as state-run PR to make the public root for the robots that will take their jobs, and argue Tesla's Optimus is well ahead with 1 billion units by 2036. The bulk of the episode is an AI-market argument: Hugging Face approached at a $13B+ valuation after Stripe's $7B Open Router deal, open source winning token share but not revenue, and app-layer companies like Harvey forking Kimi K3 for sovereignty because they can't trust frontier labs. Calacanis also makes an anti-UBI, pro-minimum-wage case ($1/year for ten years to $20/hour), pushes distributed 'porch solar' resilience against Iran-linked grid attacks, and covers the first forensically confirmed fully autonomous kill drone in Ukraine.

themes.theme: China's robot spectacle as soft power

insights.claim: At the Beijing World Humanoid Robot Games (51 events, 1,000+ competitions, held in the 2022 Winter Olympics speed skating oval), humanoid robots beat two human world records: a 100m sprint in 9.39 seconds and a 2.88m standing high jump versus Javier Sotomayor's 2.45m human mark from 1993.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: Humanoid locomotion has crossed elite-human benchmarks in narrow athletic tasks — a concrete capability marker for anyone underwriting robotics timelines.
insights.quote: One finished the 100 meter sprint in 9.39 seconds, besting Usain Bolts world record. And then another one bested the human record in the standing high jump with 2.88 meters.

insights.claim: China's robot games are deliberate labor-displacement PR: the state is manufacturing public affection for humanoids before those humanoids take jobs, and the US is losing the AI narrative war badly.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Public sentiment is the gating factor on robot deployment; markets should watch which countries can deploy humanoids without political backlash — that is a deployment-rate input, not a technology one.
insights.quote: You have to entertain people. You have to make them root for the robots

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis predicts that at next year's Beijing humanoid games, robots will break the human record in 48 of 51 event categories, up from 2 of 51 this year.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A falsifiable, dated benchmark on humanoid capability slope — if it lands anywhere near 48/51, robotics capex assumptions are too conservative.
insights.quote: Next year, I'm going to say 48 of 51 categories will be broken the human record.

insights.claim: The Beijing robot showcase is best read as military signaling toward Taiwan rather than a commercial demo — a demonstration that China could mass-produce and deploy humanoid units at scale.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Frames humanoid manufacturing capacity as a geopolitical/defense variable, relevant to Taiwan-risk pricing and to defense-robotics exposure.
insights.quote: This is a message to the rest of the world that we can send a million of these to Taiwan and take the fabs.

insights.claim: Robot sports have a structural ceiling as entertainment because spectator appeal comes from human effort and training, which robots do not have to supply.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: Argues against a durable consumer-media business built on robot competition — a caution for anyone valuing robot-entertainment IP or venues.
insights.quote: there's no discipline. There's no there's no grit or drive. It's not a It's not a good story in that way.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis, after a private viewing of an unreleased Optimus demo, says Tesla's robot is roughly a generation and a half ahead of the Chinese humanoids shown in Beijing on hardware and further ahead on the software 'brain'.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A first-hand (if non-specific) capability read that Tesla's humanoid lead is real — supports the robotics option value embedded in TSLA rather than in Chinese humanoid suppliers.
insights.quote: in addition to the hardware that I think is one and a half generations beyond these, I think the brain is like five generations behind these.

insights.claim: Calacanis predicts there will be 1 billion Optimus robots in the world by 2036 and that Optimus will be the highest-selling and highest-value product in human history, surpassing the iPhone.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: An extreme upside case for Tesla's non-auto TAM; even a 10x haircut implies humanoid volumes far above current consensus supply-chain forecasts.
insights.quote: I didn't say 1 million I didn't say 10 million I didn't say 100 million I said 1 billion

insights.claim: If Tesla entered Optimus in the Beijing humanoid games, Calacanis predicts it would win 35 of the 51 contests.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable yardstick for the Tesla-vs-China humanoid gap if Tesla ever competes publicly.

insights.claim: Tesla has repurposed its Model S and Model X production lines to build Optimus, indicating the humanoid program is consuming existing auto manufacturing capacity rather than greenfield capacity.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Implies real opportunity cost inside Tesla's auto segment and a physical commitment to humanoid volume — watch legacy sedan/SUV output as a tell.
insights.quote: they ripped out the Model X and the Model S factory lines and they're building these.

themes.theme: Hugging Face sale and the open-source layer

insights.claim: Hugging Face has been approached about a sale at a valuation above $13 billion and is taking it seriously, talking to banks about evaluating bids, versus its last raise in 2023 at a $4.5 billion post-money valuation.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: A ~3x markup in two years on the open-model distribution layer sets a comparable for AI-infrastructure marketplaces and signals an M&A window in the model-routing stack.
insights.quote: Hugging face has been approached for a sale at a valuation of over $13 billion.

insights.claim: Stripe's recent $7 billion acquisition of Open Router is the direct comparable for a Hugging Face deal, and the two products are converging: Open Router routes workloads across models while Hugging Face hosts models and datasets with a social layer.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host) and Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Model routing plus model hosting is consolidating into one category — incumbents without a routing asset (clouds, frontier labs) are the natural next bidders.
insights.quote: if open router were to add comments and a little bit more community features or hugging face were to do a little more routing. It's the same product.

insights.claim: Calacanis says the most likely acquirers of Hugging Face are hyperscalers — AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, or Nvidia — because owning the open-model repository lets them route inference traffic to their own compute.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Names the bidder set; a cloud winning Hugging Face converts a neutral repository into a demand-funnel for that cloud's inference capacity.
insights.quote: I do think AWS, Google Cloud or Azure will buy this in a heartbeat for that amount of money.

insights.claim: The 'master stroke' would be a frontier lab (Anthropic, OpenAI, or xAI) buying Hugging Face, because it would both neutralize the open-source threat and expose which customers use which open models, letting the acquirer undercut them on price at the point of choice.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A defensive-acquisition thesis with a data-advantage kicker; if it happens, open-model pricing gets weaponized and independent inference providers lose their pricing shield.
insights.quote: Then if they're watching which customers are doing which models, they can insert their model at a lower price

insights.claim: Calacanis's operating rule for platform M&A: you always buy the fastest-growing threat to your business, either to kill it or to control its data — the pattern behind Facebook/Instagram, Facebook Messenger/WhatsApp, and Google/YouTube.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A reusable screen for predicting acquisitions: identify the fastest-growing adjacent threat to each platform incumbent and price the option that it gets bought.
insights.quote: You always buy the most threatening thing to your business either to kill it or to get the data and control it.

insights.claim: Salesforce buying Hugging Face would be a credible re-rating trade, moving the company out of the 'SaaS apocalypse' narrative that is punishing its multiple and into the AI-infrastructure narrative.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis and Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: Names a specific narrative-driven acquisition that could re-rate a beaten-down SaaS megacap — watch Salesforce M&A headlines as a multiple catalyst.
insights.quote: he's getting his ass kicked in the markets because he's viewed as a SAS company.

insights.claim: Calacanis claims he called in January 2024 that open source could win the majority of AI tokens — though not the majority of revenue, since frontier models remain expensive — driven by developers' demand for sovereignty, the same dynamic that drove Hadoop and MySQL adoption in databases.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Splits the market into token share (open source) and revenue share (frontier) — the right frame for sizing inference-provider revenue versus raw usage growth.
insights.quote: I thought open source would win the majority of the tokens. not the majority of the revenue because the Frontier models are expensive

insights.claim: Frontier-model coding tools produce severe cost shock at the team level: Calacanis's company burned $2,400 of a $2,500 Claude credit grant in six weeks after enabling Claude in Slack, on top of roughly $2,500 per employee per year across about 20 people.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Real-world evidence that agentic coding spend scales unpredictably — this is the demand driver pushing buyers toward routers and cheaper open models.
insights.quote: $2,400 in the first six weeks gone.

themes.theme: Platform vs application layer and model sovereignty

insights.claim: Sam Altman says OpenAI intends to be a platform rather than a product company and will not build every product category or compete with its own customers, positioning OpenAI as the low-cost utility layer for AI.
insights.speaker: Sam Altman (clip)
insights.so_what: If taken literally, it caps OpenAI's application-layer land-grab and de-risks app-layer startups building on OpenAI relative to those building on rivals.
insights.quote: I don't think we should go build every product category. I don't think we should like go try to compete with all of our customers.

insights.claim: Calacanis reads Altman's 'we won't compete with our customers' positioning as a direct attack on Anthropic, which shipped Claude Code and Claude Design straight into its own customers' markets.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Frames a competitive wedge in enterprise AI sales: OpenAI can sell trust-not-to-compete, which matters to app-layer buyers picking a model vendor.
insights.quote: What you described to me is a direct shot at Anthropic. Anthropic created Claude Code and Claude Design. They specifically went after their customers.

insights.claim: Harvey forked the open Kimi K3 model to run its own sovereign legal AI on its own servers, so none of its usage, feedback, or output signal flows back to a frontier lab — evidence that application leaders are defecting from frontier APIs.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host) and Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A named, high-value app company choosing a forked open model over an API is the leading indicator for frontier-lab revenue leakage at the top of the customer base.
insights.quote: Kimmy K3 to make their own legal AI sovereign. They control it.

insights.claim: Calacanis's 'castle and keeps' framework: an app company that owns its forked model has a castle, and each customer's on-premise data store is a walled keep whose documents and signal never travel back up to the app vendor or to a frontier lab.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A concrete architecture for enterprise AI defensibility — vendors who can offer it will win regulated verticals; frontier labs lose the data flywheel there.

insights.claim: Application-layer companies including 11 Labs, Lovable, Lingora, and Figma increasingly fear frontier labs will copy their products, which is why they are moving toward owned models.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Names the cohort most likely to shift inference spend to open/self-hosted models — bullish for open-model tooling, bearish for frontier API growth from top accounts.
insights.quote: People are starting to realize I just can't trust the Frontier models not to steal my business.

insights.claim: Acquiring a founder can kill the product: after Sam Altman hired OpenClaw's founder Peter Steinberg in a deal Calacanis pegs at roughly $200-250 million, OpenClaw's momentum evaporated almost immediately and it stopped shipping updates while Hermes, Perplexity Computer, and Grokbot took the agent conversation.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Acqui-hiring the founder is a cheaper competitive kill than buying the company — a pattern to watch when a hot open-source project's founder takes a lab job.
insights.quote: the purchase of open claw's founder killed openclaw let me just say it clearly folks I predicted it

insights.claim: Calacanis believes Nvidia's Jensen Huang was visibly irritated that OpenAI announced an Nvidia deal and then an AMD deal within roughly two weeks, and speculates Jensen may not have exercised his multi-billion-dollar option to invest in OpenAI as a result.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: If the Nvidia-OpenAI investment option goes unexercised, it would be a meaningful signal about the durability of the vendor-financing loop in AI compute.

insights.claim: Calacanis, a self-described capitalist, argues UBI will never pass in America and is the wrong answer, and instead proposes a coordinated corporate commitment to raise the bottom wage by $1 per year for ten years, from roughly $7 to $20 an hour.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A named alternative to the UBI narrative that AI labs use to defuse job-loss fear; if the elite consensus shifts toward wage floors, low-wage employers and staffing-heavy retail/logistics names carry the cost.
insights.quote: UBI UBI is a road to nowhere. I just take it out of your mind for it's it's about the minimum wage.

insights.claim: Calacanis cites minimum-wage studies from Australia, New Zealand, Seattle and New York showing gradual increases cost less than 1-2% of jobs and pass through only 1-3% to consumer prices, and says only about 15 million Americans earn under $15 an hour.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: The economic-impact numbers he anchors on are small enough that a coordinated wage floor is financeable — a policy scenario to price into low-wage-employer margins.
insights.quote: you lose less than one or two% of jobs to automation, and the price of a burger goes up one, two, or 3%.

insights.claim: A worker moving to $20/hour and 2,000 hours clears roughly $40,000 and crosses the benefit cliff off food stamps and housing subsidies, which means today's low wage floor is effectively a taxpayer subsidy to large employers.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Reframes wage policy as a transfer from taxpayers to employers — the political framing most likely to move corporate wage policy, and a fiscal-cost argument that can cut both ways.

insights.claim: Calacanis singles out Amazon for using delivery service partners to suppress wages while he is simultaneously a large and increasing shareholder because he considers it one of the best-run companies in the world.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: An explicit disclosure that a vocal wage-floor advocate is adding to Amazon — the labor critique is not, in his view, an investment thesis against it.
insights.quote: I'm a very large shareholder in Amazon. And I'm increasing my ownership in Amazon

insights.claim: Coordination is the binding constraint on wage increases: a single company that raises pay, like Starbucks, is put at a cost disadvantage to rivals such as Dutch Bros, so only an industry-wide commitment works.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Explains why voluntary wage floors fail absent a schelling point — relevant to modeling whether any single retailer's wage move sticks.

insights.claim: Calacanis frames a modest wage floor as insurance against violent anti-elite backlash, and argues higher bottom-decile wages are pro-capitalist because that cohort saves nothing and spends 100% of income, raising monetary velocity.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A demand-side argument that wage increases flow straight into consumer subscriptions and retail — the offsetting revenue line to the margin hit.
insights.quote: Would you rather have them sharpening the guillotines and firebombing CEO's houses and shooting CEOs in the back of the head gangland style?

insights.claim: Sam Altman concedes the AI industry has communicated badly about job losses and data centers, and Calacanis argues the winning message is a permanent free unlimited tier — a free tutor and medical second opinion for every human — rather than UBI studies.
insights.speaker: Sam Altman (clip) and Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: The messaging pivot to come from AI labs; a permanent free consumer tier is a real cost commitment that shapes consumer-AI monetization assumptions.
insights.quote: We have not as a field done a very good job of explaining to people what the benefits are and how the downsides can be mitigated

insights.claim: The co-host argues the opposite case on UBI: freeing people from subsistence work would unlock new businesses and industries, and the small share who opt out entirely is a cheaper outcome than crime or dependency — but agrees America has no political appetite for it.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: Marks where the disagreement actually sits: both hosts expect UBI to fail politically regardless of merit, so plan for wage-floor fights, not transfer programs.

insights.claim: An Iran-linked cyberattack shut down a small UK power plant for four days in July, and the FBI has warned of Iran-linked attackers targeting US water facilities in at least seven states.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: Concrete escalation of state-linked attacks on Western utilities — supports the case for OT/critical-infrastructure security spend and utility resilience capex.
insights.quote: a small UK power plant was shut down for 4 days in July following a cyber attack linked to Iran.

insights.claim: Calacanis's core resilience thesis: capitalism optimizes to a single cheapest system, which is exactly what makes supply chains and grids attackable, so the fix is deliberate redundancy at every level — the same lesson as concentrating medicine and PPE manufacturing in China.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: The reshoring/redundancy trade restated as a security requirement rather than a political one — durable demand for duplicate capacity even where it is uneconomic.
insights.quote: In capitalism, we like to build one system because it is more affordable.

insights.claim: 'Porch solar' — plug-in balcony solar panels with suitcase-sized batteries, now sold by IKEA in Europe for roughly 500 euros and up — is the emerging consumer resilience product, at around $1,000 self-installed versus $10,000-20,000 for an installed natural gas or kerosene generator.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A 10-20x cheaper, no-installer entry point into home backup power that could take share from home standby generators and shave peak grid load; watch IKEA's rollout as a category signal.
insights.quote: These solar panels and batteries are $1,000. You install it yourself.

insights.claim: Every plug-in solar-plus-battery install both protects the household during an outage and takes marginal load off a grid that will be persistently stressed, making distributed generation a load-relief mechanism rather than only a backup product.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: If adoption scales, it dents peak-load growth forecasts that utilities and IPPs are using to justify capacity buildouts.

insights.claim: Middle-class households in Texas are already buying solar plus batteries (roughly $10,000-20,000) and rainwater collection tanks after the 2021 freeze, showing resilience spending has moved down-market from preppers to ordinary homeowners.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Demand for home resilience hardware is a real consumer category now — relevant to residential solar, storage, and water-equipment demand in deregulated/fragile grid states.

insights.claim: A small Russian drone that struck a gas station in Zaporizhzhia last month, killing three people including a 19-year-old student, is assessed by drone experts, Ukrainian commanders, and a forensic team to have been fully autonomous — given a general target area and then selecting its own aim point.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: First forensic evidence of machine target selection in the field — an inflection for autonomous-weapons regulation, defense procurement, and AI-lab policy positions.
insights.quote: In a few years, we believe we will be living in a Terminator movie. It's no joke. Machines are making decisions to strike.

insights.claim: Ukraine has become one of the most capable drone powers alongside the US and China and is now an exporter, with American billionaires including Eric Schmidt investing in Ukrainian drone and counter-drone companies such as Kyiv-based Reream.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Ukraine is now a supply source, not just a demand sink, for drone tech — a specific venture pipeline in defense hardware worth tracking.

insights.claim: The most practical counter-drone measures today are low-tech nets strung over buildings and streets plus AI-directed swarms of tiny kamikaze interceptor drones, of the kind used in Kimbal Musk's drone-show business.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Counter-drone value may accrue to cheap kinetic and physical solutions rather than expensive directed-energy systems — a screen for defense-tech investment.
insights.quote: One of the greatest ways to stop drones is nets.

insights.claim: A Taiwan conflict would likely be fought as AI drones and robots launched from container ships against each other, with humans largely removed from direct combat.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Shapes what defense spending a Taiwan scenario would actually pull forward: autonomy, launch platforms, and counter-swarm, not traditional platforms.

insights.claim: Mandalorian and Grogu grossed $345 million worldwide against a $145-165 million budget before marketing and came in below Disney's own expectations, in the first theatrical Star Wars release since Rise of Skywalker in 2019.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: A concrete underperformance datapoint on Disney's most valuable franchise, with the Disney+ slate also thinning — relevant to Disney content-ROI and franchise-value assumptions.
insights.quote: only gross 345 million worldwide in theaters. Even Disney conceds it came in below expectations.

insights.claim: The co-host's contrarian read is that Star Wars fandom has always oscillated between adoration and revulsion for each new release, so the current 'franchise is dead' consensus is a narrow-window error rather than a structural decline.
insights.speaker: Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: Argues against marking down franchise IP on a single soft release — a sentiment-versus-fundamentals distinction for media asset valuation.

insights.claim: Disney's Star Wars turnaround depends on Dave Filoni, now running the franchise creatively, reverting to Clone Wars-era material and original-trilogy character continuity, with the next theatrical release the Ryan Gosling Starfighter film in May 2027.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis and Lon (co-host)
insights.so_what: The dated catalyst and creative-leadership change to watch for any Disney franchise-recovery thesis.
